## Comprehension questions

> "*Why does difficulty increase as the level of required reproducibility increase for a data science project. In your day-to-day work, what’s the hardest reproducibility challenge?*"

Each layer of the environment we need to reproduce adds work, and the work grows faster than the payoff. Packages are cheap to capture: `renv.lock` or `requirements.txt` records them, and one command restores them. The system layer is harder, because a lockfile can record the R version but can't install it or the operating system underneath it. At the far end, some regulated industries have to rerun an analysis exactly a decade later, which means keeping the physical hardware running. That's why the chapter calls a completely reproducible environment "a fool's errand."

The hardest challenge I've run into is in the system layer. It's impossible to know what system requirements developers might need (for both Python and R), and you might not have the level of control you want on the server. 

> "*There’s a table of the layers of the data science environment above. It names six items across three layers. Draw a mental map of the relationships between these six items. Pay particular attention to why the higher layers depend on the lower ones.*"

Each item is built for, or runs on, the item below it, so a change at the bottom reaches everything above it:

Packages are built for a specific language version and operating system, and many of them link to system libraries (`{sf}` needs GDAL, for example). The R and Python interpreters and the system libraries are compiled for the operating system. The operating system runs on virtual hardware (an EC2 instance), and the virtual hardware runs on physical servers in a data center. Also, having old system libraries on the operating system can be enough to block R installations.

> "*What are the two key attributes of environments as code? Why do you need both of them? Are there cases where you might only care about one?*"

Isolation and portability. The package environment is isolated, so other work on the same machine can't disrupt it, and it can be captured and moved to another machine. These are the first two takeaways in [Project-oriented workflows](#project-oriented-workflows) below.

Each one protects something different. Isolation keeps the project working when I update a package for another project. Capturing the environment lets a colleague, a server, or me in six months rebuild it.

Sometimes one is enough. A throwaway analysis I'll delete next week needs isolation but not a lockfile. Inside a container, the container already provides the isolation, so the lockfile is the part I still need.

> "*Draw a mental map of the relationships between the following: package repository, package library, package, project-level-library, .libPaths() (R) or sys.path (Python), lockfile.*"

The `renv` and `venv` diagrams below map these items. A package repository (CRAN or PyPI) holds the current and archived versions of each package. Installing a package puts one version in a package library, which holds at most one version of each package. Libraries can be system, user, or project level, and a project-level library holds one project's packages.

`.libPaths()` (R) and `sys.path` (Python) list the libraries in search order. Activating `renv` or `venv` puts the project-level library first. The lockfile (`renv.lock` or `requirements.txt`) records each package and its version, so we can rebuild the library from the repository.

> "*Why is it a bad idea to share package libraries? What’s the best way to collaborate with a colleague using an environment as code? What commands will you run in R or Python to save a package environment and restore it later?*"

Package installs are specific to the operating system and language version, so a library built on my laptop might not work on a colleague's machine. Package files are also large. It's much easier to share a lockfile instead: keep `renv.lock` or `requirements.txt` in Git, and each machine installs its own packages from it.

In R, `renv::snapshot()` saves the environment and `renv::restore()` restores it. In Python, `python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt` saves it and `python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt` restores it.

## Project-oriented workflows

Key takeaways: 

1. Each project should have an **isolated** package environment that preserves the names and versions. 

2. The project's dependencies/requirements should be captured in a way that **makes it exportable/transferable to another machine**.[^renv-venv]

3. Each project should have a **virtual environment** in a **standalone directory** that documents everything the project needs (usually in a GitHub or GitLab repo).[^rstats-wtf-projects]

[^rstats-wtf-projects]: Read more in [What They Forgot to Teach You About R: Chapter 3, Project-oriented workflow](https://rstats.wtf/projects)

[^renv-venv]: In R, this is [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html). In Python, this is [`venv`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment).

## Virtual environments

As [do4ds notes](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-1-env-as-code.html), `venv` and `renv` "*keep user-level package caches of the actual packages and use symlinks, so only one copy of the package is installed.*"

### `renv`

First, read the documentation on [project level management with `renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html) and [using renv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-renv).

I’ve summarized the steps below:

1. Create a new R project-local environment

    ```r
    install.packages("renv")
    renv::init()
    ```

2. Install packages into the renv-managed environment

    ```r
    install.packages(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2"))
    ```

3. Snapshot the state of the environment and package versions in the lock file (`renv.lock`)

    ```r
    renv::snapshot()
    ```

4. To deactivate the environment, close the R session. `renv` projects are automatically reactivated the next time the project is opened. Restore the environment on a new system with:

    ```r
    renv::restore()
    ```

#### The `renv-eda-basic` project

To demonstrate how to use `renv`, I've copied the `eda-basic.qmd` file into its own project folder (`renv-eda-basic`):

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
_labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/
└── eda-basic.qmd
```

:::

Then I ran `renv::init()`: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::init()
```

```{r}
#| collapse: true
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
fs::dir_tree(
  path = "_labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/", 
  all = TRUE, 
  recurse = 1)
```

Initiating `renv` in a project root directory will create the `.Rprofile` and `renv.lock` files and a `renv/` folder:

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
_labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/
├── .Rprofile
├── .gitignore
├── eda-basic.qmd
├── renv
│   ├── .gitignore
│   ├── activate.R
│   └── settings.json
├── renv-eda-basic.Rproj
└── renv.lock
```

:::

The `renv-eda-basic.Rproj` file comes from RStudio, not `renv::init()`. It helps enforce project-oriented workflows (but `.Rproj` files are specific to RStudio).  

To install the packages, we can use `install.packages()` or `pak::pak()` for more flexible installations:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2"))
```

```{r}
#| label: co_box_renv_install
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "b",
  look = "default", 
  hsize = "1.25", 
  size = "1.00", 
  header = "**Note**", 
  fold = FALSE,
  contents = "In an `renv` project, `install.packages()` calls `renv::install()`, which uses cached packages when available. Otherwise, it installs the latest version from CRAN.")
```

Create a snapshot (i.e., the current versions of R and any installed packages, along with the R repositories) with `renv::snapshot()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::snapshot()
```

The dependencies are saved in the `renv.lock` file, which should be committed to version control. 

To make sure the dependencies in the `renv.lock` file have been installed (i.e., after cloning), run: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::restore()
```

### `venv`

Read the [documentation on Python virtual environments](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment) and using [venv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-venv). 

I've summarized the steps below:

1. Create new Python 3 virtual environment in the `.venv` directory 

    ```bash
    python3 -m venv .venv
    ```

2. Activate the environment

    ```bash
    source .venv/bin/activate
    ```

3. Use `pip` to install packages into your environment

    ```bash
    python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas
    ```

4. Deactivate an environment

    ```bash 
    deactivate
    ```

5. Save environment

    ```bash
    python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
    ```

6. Restoring environment

    ```bash 
    python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
    ```

#### The `venv-model-basic-py` project

Use the **Terminal** to navigate to the `venv-model-basic-py` folder and create the Python virtual environment: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
python3 -m venv .venv
```

This will create a `.venv/` folder inside `venv-model-basic-py`.

To activate the virtual environment, run the following in the **Terminal**:

```{bash}

```

This should change the **Terminal** prompt from: 

```{bash}

Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$ 
```

to: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
(.venv) Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$
```

Now we can install the required Python packages (we include `jupyter` for interactive outputs):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
pip install palmerpenguins pandas numpy scikit-learn jupyter
```

To store the installed packages, save them to a `requirements.txt` file with `pip freeze`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

#### Rendering with Python

To render, use the following in the **Terminal**: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
quarto preview model-basic-py.qmd --no-browser --no-watch-inputs
```

Quarto uses the first Python on the `PATH`, so rendering with the virtual environment active uses `.venv`. Or we can set the Python interpreter with the `QUARTO_PYTHON` environment variable in the **Terminal**:[^venv-win]

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
export QUARTO_PYTHON="${PWD}/.venv/bin/python3"
```

[^venv-win]: On Windows try `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`


If you're working inside **RStudio or Posit Workbench**, consider letting `reticulate` manage the Python environment:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("myenv", required = TRUE)
virtualenv_install(
  envname = "myenv", 
  packages = c("palmerpenguins", "pandas", "numpy", 
               "scikit-learn", "jupyter"))
```

This ensures RStudio uses a known-good Python environment.

Now, if we open the `model-basic-py.qmd` file in RStudio and click the **Render** button in the toolbar we should see the rendered output.

## Recap

1. Each project gets its own isolated, transferable package environment. In R, `renv::init()` creates the project library and `renv.lock`, `renv::snapshot()` records the package versions, and `renv::restore()` reinstalls them on another machine.

2. In Python, `python3 -m venv .venv` creates the environment and `source .venv/bin/activate` turns it on. `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures the installed packages, and `pip install -r requirements.txt` restores them.

3. Quarto has to be told which Python interpreter to use. We can render with the virtual environment active, set `QUARTO_PYTHON` to `.venv/bin/python3` in the Terminal, or let `reticulate` manage the environment inside RStudio.

Next, [Modeling in Python](model-basic-py.qmd) walks through the code in `model-basic-py.qmd`.
